title: The Great Molasses Flood (1919) — The Real Reason It Was Deadly
parts: In 1919, a wave of molasses rolling through Boston at 35 miles an hour killed 21 people.
For almost a hundred years, nobody could fully explain why something that slow could be that deadly.
Then a Harvard physics class ran the numbers.
This is the story of a tank that should never have been built, and the cold night that made it worse.
January 15th, 1919. Boston's North End.
A steel tank, five stories tall, held over two million gallons of molasses.
Just after noon, it tore open.
Twenty-one people died. About 150 were hurt.
The wave was fast, loud, and strong enough to crush buildings along the waterfront.
Here's the part that gets skipped: the tank was never going to hold.
It was built in 1915 by a company treasurer with no engineering background.
He skipped basic safety checks, like filling it with water first to test for leaks.
The tank leaked almost from day one.
The company painted it brown, so the leaking molasses wouldn't show.
Neighborhood kids used to come and scrape up the molasses that seeped out.
An engineering review decades later found the steel walls were far too thin.
One analysis, by engineer Ronald Mayville, put it almost half as thick as it should have been.
The steel was also low in manganese, which made it brittle instead of flexible.
Mayville's own conclusion was blunt: the tank was under-designed.
After the disaster, the company had a different story.
They blamed anarchists. They said a bomb had destroyed the tank.
It wasn't a wild claim for the time — bombings by radical groups were in the news that year.
But the courts didn't buy it.
A court-appointed investigator spent almost three years on the case.
His conclusion: no bomb. No sabotage.
Just a tank that was built badly and never properly tested.
The company paid out over 600,000 dollars to victims and their families.
And Massachusetts rewrote its building codes because of it.
From then on, structures like that needed a licensed architect and engineer to sign off.
So the tank itself: that mystery was solved by 1925.
But one question stayed open for almost a century.
Molasses is slow. So why couldn't people just get out of the way?
In 2016, a Harvard fluid dynamics class decided to find out.
Nicole Sharp, Jordan Kennedy, and Shmuel Rubinstein presented their findings to the American Physical Society.
They pulled historical weather data for Boston on January 15th, 1919.
They studied molasses at different temperatures, using corn syrup in a freezer to model it.
Here's the twist: the night after the flood, temperatures dropped to near freezing.
According to their model, that cold could have made the spilled molasses four times more viscous, almost overnight.
Thicker, stickier, harder to escape, and harder to pull people out of.
Rubinstein put it simply: on a warmer day, the molasses would have spread thinner, and probably killed fewer people.
By his estimate, about half the victims died because they got stuck.
So here's the distinction worth remembering.
Why the tank broke: bad engineering, from 1915.
Why the wave was so deadly: the cold, four years before anyone built a model to explain it.
Two different questions. Two different answers.
No peer-reviewed paper on this has ever been published — just that one conference talk in 2016.
But its explanation lined up with eyewitness accounts from almost a hundred years earlier.
A badly-built tank. A company that blamed the wrong people. And a cold front that turned a disaster into a tragedy.
So next time someone says "slow as molasses," remember: for one night in Boston, slow was exactly what made it deadly.
What else gets blamed on the wrong cause, decades after the fact?
